problems.prompt: Thermionic emission is best described as:
choices: Electrons escaping a hot cathode after gaining enough thermal energy to overcome the work function
Electrons tunneling through an insulator at any temperature
Photons ejecting electrons from a cold metal surface
Electrons emitted only when the metal is negatively charged
problems.explain: Heating the cathode lets the high-energy tail of the electron thermal distribution climb over the work function barrier W and leave the surface.

problems.prompt: According to J = A T² e^(−W/k_BT), which change increases the saturated current density J the most?
choices: Raising T (since W/k_BT sits in the exponent)
problems.explain: Because W/(k_BT) is in the exponent, J is extremely sensitive to T; raising W instead strongly suppresses emission.

problems.prompt: At low anode voltage the diode current is limited by the electron cloud near the cathode repelling further emission — this regime is called ____-limited.
problems.explain: At low V the current follows the Child-Langmuir V^1.5 law (space-charge-limited); at high V it saturates at the Richardson value (temperature-limited).

problems.prompt: Using A = 6.0×10⁵ A/(m²·K²), T = 2000 K, W = 4.5 eV, k_B = 1.380649×10⁻²³ J/K, and 1 eV = 1.602176634×10⁻¹⁹ J, estimate J = A T² e^(−W/k_BT) in A/m² (answer as a power of 10, e.g. enter the coefficient rounded to 1 decimal times 10^n as a decimal number).
problems.explain: W/(k_BT) = (4.5·1.602e-19)/(1.38e-23·2000) ≈ 26.1, so J ≈ 6.0e5 · (2000)² · e^(−26.1) ≈ 11 A/m² — a small but nonzero saturated current density at this temperature and work function.
